For any non-loopback deployment,\nterminate HTTPS at a reverse proxy or private tunnel and expose only the API/UI\nport. Keep the ACP bridge on loopback.\n\nForwarding headers are ignored unless the socket peer matches an explicit\ncomma-separated `OMNIHARNESS_TRUSTED_PROXIES` rule. Rules may be exact IPs or\nIPv4 CIDRs:\n\n```text\nOMNIHARNESS_TRUSTED_PROXIES=127.0.0.1,10.20.0.0/16\nOMNIHARNESS_PUBLIC_ORIGIN=https://runner.example.net\n```\n\nConfigure the proxy to replace, not append untrusted client values for,\n`Forwarded`/`X-Forwarded-*`. Never use a catch-all trusted-proxy range.\n\n## Backup and restore\n\nStop the runner before a filesystem backup. Copy the entire instance directory,\nincluding the database, auth key, worker streams, locks, settings, and managed\nmetadata. Exclude only transient build caches. Also back up the deployment's\npassword-hash configuration separately.\n\nRestore into an empty instance path while the runner is stopped, preserve file\npermissions, then start it with the same `OMNIHARNESS_ROOT` and\n`OMNIHARNESS_INSTANCE`. The auth key is required to read encrypted settings and\nvalidate existing sessions. If it is intentionally omitted, rotate the\npassword and expect every client to authenticate again.\n\nClient profile lists and platform-secure bearer sessions are client state, not\npart of a runner backup.\n\n## Disposable smoke check\n\nThis uses an isolated root and a hidden prompt. <!-- codex-event:{"kind":"progress","timestamp":"2026-08-16T11:51:53.756Z","phase":"commentary"} -->
## Codex progress · 2026-08-16T11:51:53.756Z

I found the cause: at 13:47:57 the runner crashed on an unhandled `SQLITE_BUSY` (“database is locked”) while its watchdog was cleaning up scheduled wake records. The restart controller stayed alive, but it does not automatically supervise this kind of later crash, so port 3050 remained down.

I’m restoring service now, then I’ll harden this crash path with a regression test. I’m using the project’s backend reliability and test-first guidance because this is a real process-killing failure, not just a one-off restart.

    "text": "---\nname: test-driven-development\ndescription: Use when implementing any feature or bugfix, before writing implementation code\n---\n\n# Test-Driven Development (TDD)\n\n## Overview\n\nWrite the test first. Watch it fail. Write minimal code to pass.\n\n**Core principle:** If you didn't watch the test fail, you don't know if it tests the right thing.\n\n**Violating the letter of the rules is violating the spirit of the rules.**\n\n## When to Use\n\n**Always:**\n- New features\n- Bug fixes\n- Refactoring\n- Behavior changes\n\n**Exceptions (ask your human partner):**\n- Throwaway prototypes\n- Generated code\n- Configuration files\n\n**Do directly with targeted verification:**\n- tiny color, spacing, copy, or label changes,\n- one-line prompt wording changes,\n- docs-only wording changes,\n- mechanical edits where the expected result is obvious from the diff.\n\nDo not perform a full red-green cycle for a tiny mechanical edit unless it changes behavior or there is a real regression risk. For example, changing a button from gray to blue usually needs the edit plus a targeted visual or code check, not a new failing test.\n\nThinking \"skip TDD just this once\"? Stop. That's rationalization.\n\n## UI-Specific Note\n\nWhen the task is UI work, choose the design system and starting block before writing tests around the intended behavior and rendering. In Ultrapowers, that means `shadcn/ui` plus the closest available ShadCN Block for each new screen, form, or major surface unless the user says otherwise. Inspect https://ui.shadcn.com/blocks first, install or copy the selected block, and then adapt it. Before adding any individual control, check whether `shadcn/ui` already provides a suitable control and use/customize that control first.\n\nFor important app workflows, also consider whether `agentic-user-journey-testing` should be proposed. Do not run that higher-cost black-box test mode without explicit user approval.\n\n## The Iron Law\n\n```\nNO PRODUCTION CODE WITHOUT A FAILING TEST FIRST\n```\n\nWrite code before the test? Delete it. Start over.\n\n**No exceptions:**\n- Don't keep it as \"reference\"\n- Don't \"adapt\" it while writing tests\n- Don't look at it\n- Delete means delete\n\nImplement fresh from tests. Period.\n\n## Red-Green-Refactor\n\n```dot\ndigraph tdd_cycle {\n    rankdir=LR;\n    red [label=\"RED\\nWrite failing test\", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor=\"#ffcccc\"];\n    verify_red [label=\"Verify fails\\ncorrectly\", shape=diamond];\n    green [label=\"GREEN\\nMinimal code\", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor=\"#ccffcc\"];\n    verify_green [label=\"Verify passes\\nAll green\", shape=diamond];\n    refactor [label=\"REFACTOR\\nClean up\", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor=\"#ccccff\"];\n    next [label=\"Next\", shape=ellipse];\n\n    red -> verify_red;\n    verify_red -> green [label=\"yes\"];\n    verify_red -> red [label=\"wrong\\nfailure\"];\n    green -> verify_green;\n    verify_green -> refactor [label=\"yes\"];\n    verify_green -> green [label=\"no\"];\n    refactor -> verify_green [label=\"stay\\ngreen\"];\n    verify_green -> next;\n    next -> red;\n}\n```\n\n### RED - Write Failing Test\n\nWrite one minimal test showing what should happen.\n\n<Good>\n```typescript\ntest('retries failed operations 3 times', async () => {\n  let attempts = 0;\n  const operation = () => {\n    attempts++;\n    if (attempts < 3) throw new Error('fail');\n    return 'success';\n  };\n\n  const result = await retryOperation(operation);\n\n  expect(result).toBe('success');\n  expect(attempts).toBe(3);\n});\n```\nClear name, tests real behavior, one thing\n</Good>\n\n<Bad>\n```typescript\ntest('retry works', async () => {\n  const mock = jest.fn()\n    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())\n    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())\n    .mockResolvedValueOnce('success');\n  await retryOperation(mock);\n  expect(mock).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);\n});\n```\nVague name, tests mock not code\n</Bad>\n\n**Requirements:**\n- One behavior\n- Clear name\n- Real code (no mocks unless unavoidable)\n- Real product behavior is the target. Mocked behavior can never be the final deliverable or proof that the feature works.\n\n### Verify RED - Watch It Fail\n\n**MANDATORY. Never skip.**\n\n```bash\nnpm test path/to/test.test.ts\n```\n\nConfirm:\n- Test fails (not errors)\n- Failure message is expected\n- Fails because feature missing (not typos)\n\n**Test passes?** You're testing existing behavior. Fix test.\n\n**Test errors?** Fix error, re-run until it fails correctly.\n\n### GREEN - Minimal Code\n\nWrite simplest code to pass the test.\n\n<Good>\n```typescript\nasync function retryOperation<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {\n  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {\n    try {\n      return await fn();\n    } catch (e) {\n      if (i === 2) throw e;\n    }\n  }\n  throw new Error('unreachable');\n}\n```\nJust enough to pass\n</Good>\n\n<Bad>\n```typescript\nasync function retryOperation<T>(\n  fn: () => Promise<T>,\n  options?: {\n    maxRetries?: number;\n    backoff?: 'linear' | 'exponential';\n    onRetry?: (attempt: number) => void;\n  }\n): Promise<T> {\n  // YAGNI\n}\n```\nOver-engineered\n</Bad>\n\nDon't add features, refactor other code, or \"improve\" beyond the test.\n\n### Verify GREEN - Watch It Pass\n\n**MANDATORY.**\n\n```bash\nnpm test path/to/test.test.ts\n```\n\nConfirm:\n- Test passes\n- Other tests still pass\n- Output pristine (no errors, warnings)\n\n**Test fails?** Fix code, not test.\n\n**Other tests fail?** Fix now.\n\n### REFACTOR - Clean Up\n\nAfter green only:\n- Remove duplication\n- Improve names\n- Extract helpers\n\nKeep tests green. Don't add behavior.\n\n### Repeat\n\nNext failing test for next feature.\n\n## Good Tests\n\n| Quality | Good | Bad |\n|---------|------|-----|\n| **Minimal** | One thing. \"and\" in name? Split it. | `test('validates email and domain and whitespace')` |\n| **Clear** | Name describes behavior | `test('test1')` |\n| **Shows intent** | Demonstrates desired API | Obscures what code should do |\n\n## Why Order Matters\n\n**\"I'll write tests after to verify it works\"**\n\nTests written after code pass immediately. Passing immediately proves nothing:\n- Might test wrong thing\n- Might test implementation, not behavior\n- Might miss edge cases you forgot\n- You never saw it catch the bug\n\nTest-first forces you to see the test fail, proving it actually tests something.\n\n**\"I already manually tested all the edge cases\"**\n\nManual testing is ad-hoc. You think you tested everything but:\n- No record of what you tested\n- Can't re-run when code changes\n- Easy to forget cases under pressure\n- \"It worked when I tried it\" ≠ comprehensive\n\nAutomated tests are systematic. They run the same way every time.\n\n**\"Deleting X hours of work is wasteful\"**\n\nSunk cost fallacy. The time is already gone. Your choice now:\n- Delete and rewrite with TDD (X more hours, high confidence)\n- Keep it and add tests after (30 min, low confidence, likely bugs)\n\nThe \"waste\" is keeping code you can't trust. Working code without real tests is technical debt.\n\n**\"TDD is dogmatic, being pragmatic means adapting\"**\n\nTDD IS pragmatic:\n- Finds bugs before commit (faster than debugging after)\n- Prevents regressions (tests catch breaks immediately)\n- Documents behavior (tests show how to use code)\n- Enables refactoring (change freely, tests catch breaks)\n\n\"Pragmatic\" shortcuts = debugging in production = slower.\n\n**\"Tests after achieve the same goals - it's spirit not ritual\"**\n\nNo. Tests-after answer \"What does this do?\" Tests-first answer \"What should this do?\"\n\nTests-after are biased by your implementation. You test what you built, not what's required. You verify remembered edge cases, not discovered ones.\n\nTests-first force edge case discovery before implementing. Tests-after verify you remembered everything (you didn't).\n\n30 minutes of tests after ≠ TDD. You get coverage, lose proof tests work.\n\n## Common Rationalizations\n\n| Excuse | Reality |\n|--------|---------|\n| \"Too simple to test\" | Simple code breaks. Test takes 30 seconds. |\n| \"I'll test after\" | Tests passing immediately prove nothing. |\n| \"Tests after achieve same goals\" | Tests-after = \"what does this do?\" Tests-first = \"what should this do?\" |\n| \"Already manually tested\" | Ad-hoc ≠ systematic. No record, can't re-run. |\n| \"Deleting X hours is wasteful\" | Sunk cost fallacy. Keeping unverified code is technical debt. |\n| \"Keep as reference, write tests first\" | You'll adapt it. That's testing after. Delete means delete. |\n| \"Need to explore first\" | Fine. Throw away exploration, start with TDD. |\n| \"Test hard = design unclear\" | Listen to test. Hard to test = hard to use. |\n| \"TDD will slow me down\" | TDD faster than debugging. Pragmatic = test-first. |\n| \"Manual test faster\" | Manual doesn't prove edge cases. You'll re-test every change. |\n| \"Existing code has no tests\" | You're improving it. Add tests for existing code. |\n\n## Red Flags - STOP and Start Over\n\n- Code before test\n- Test after implementation\n- Test passes immediately\n- Can't explain why test failed\n- Tests added \"later\"\n- Rationalizing \"just this once\"\n- \"I already manually tested it\"\n- \"Tests after achieve the same purpose\"\n- \"It's about spirit not ritual\"\n- \"Keep as reference\" or \"adapt existing code\"\n- \"Already spent X hours, deleting is wasteful\"\n- \"TDD is dogmatic, I'm being pragmatic\"\n- \"This is different because...\"\n\n**All of these mean: Delete code. Start over with TDD.**\n\n## Example: Bug Fix\n\n**Bug:** Empty email accepted\n\n**RED**\n```typescript\ntest('rejects empty email', async () => {\n  const result = await submitForm({ email: '' });\n  expect(result.error).toBe('Email required');\n});\n```\n\n**Verify RED**\n```bash\n$ npm test\nFAIL: expected 'Email required', got undefined\n---\nname: instrumenting-control-planes\ndescription: Use when building, planning, reviewing, or debugging apps with backend decisions, agent workflows, long-running jobs, SSE/WebSocket streams, recovery paths, deletes, retries, or user-visible failures\n---\n\n# Instrumenting Control Planes\n\nBuild the control plane as a product surface. If the server decides, refuses, retries, spawns, deletes, recovers, gives up, or fails, that decision must be observable by users, operators, and tests.\n\nIf a React UI consumes the control plane through server state, optimistic UI, caches, polling, SSE/WebSocket streams, or persisted runtime state, also use `client-server-state-invariants`.\n\n## Core Rule\n\nEvery meaningful server-side state transition emits a named, durable event. The UI and tests consume the same production event surface.\n\nDo not rely on snapshot diffs, rendered DOM state, logs only, or client-side re-derivation to prove what the server decided.\n\n## Hot Path Rule\n\nNo user bootstrap, catalog, status, reconnect, or recovery request may depend on a lock-prone database write path or external health probe finishing. Serve these paths from a bounded read model, memory cache, append-only event log, or stale-but-marked snapshot; queue reconciliation writes outside the request. Every dependency on a database or bridge call in a hot path needs a short timeout, cancellation, and an explicit degraded response.\n\nIf SQLite, local files, or a single-writer store is used, assume writer contention can freeze readers at the worst moment. Use one writer, WAL/busy-timeout discipline, short transactions, bounded queues, and headless chaos tests that run bootstrap/reload while writes are active. A 25s UI request is a control-plane failure, even if the database eventually returns.\n\n## Event Contract\n\nFor each backend or agent workflow, define:\n\n- named events for decisions: `worker.spawned`, `worker.reattached`, `plan.ready`, `plan.review.blocked`, `recovery.gave_up`, `conversation.delete_failed`;\n- payloads with stable ids, `prev`/`next` status when relevant, reason codes, and enough context to debug;\n- `error.surfaced` or an equivalent user-facing failure event for every failure the user should know about;\n- durable persistence or a bounded replay buffer so short disconnects do not erase history;\n- a scriptable read path: CLI, HTTP endpoint, sqlite query, or event log command.\n\nIf a decision cannot be asserted from this surface, the design is incomplete.\n\nIf debugging a control-plane failure reveals a reusable lesson, use `ultrapowers:learning-from-bugs` after the fix is verified.\n\n## Streaming Requirements\n\nFor SSE or WebSocket-like streams:\n\n- emit named events alongside any snapshot/update frame;\n- include monotonic event ids;\n- support resume from the last seen id;\n- replay missed events from a bounded buffer;\n- emit an explicit resync-required event when replay is impossible;\n- bootstrap from a snapshot, then tail events.\n\nSnapshots show current truth. Named events show why it became true.\n\n## Testing Standard\n\nControl-plane tests should usually be headless HTTP/SSE scenario tests, not browser tests. Browser automation is for UI behavior; control-plane tests assert server decisions directly.\n\nWrite scenario assertions as event transcripts:\n\n```ts\nexpect(events).toHaveEmitted(\"worker.spawned\", { runId });\nexpect(events).toHaveEmitted(\"worker.status\", { next: \"running\" });\nchaos.killServer();\nchaos.restartServer();\nexpect(events).toHaveEmitted(\"worker.reattached\", { runId });\nexpect(events).not.toHaveEmitted(\"worker.recreated\", { runId });\n```\n\nChaos belongs outside production code paths: drop connections in the client, fail fetches in the harness, restart the server process, and use seeds for reproducibility.\n\n## Refuse These Shapes\n\n- silent early returns in server methods;\n- swallowed `catch` blocks;\n- client-side derivation of server decisions;\n- response-code-only user failures;\n- event streams without ids or resume;\n- tests that infer control-plane behavior from rendered state;\n- delete handlers that do not enumerate dependent rows or emit typed failure events;\n- recovery loops without terminal events such as `gave_up` or `abandoned`;\n- request handlers that wait on inline reconciliation writes, SQLite contention, or bridge `/doctor` checks before returning bootstrap data;\n- test-only behavior branches in production code.\n\n## Design Checklist\n\nBefore implementing a backend or agent workflow, answer:\n\n1. What decisions can this workflow make?\n2. What named event is emitted for each decision, including refusal and failure?\n3. Where are events persisted or buffered?\n4. How does a client resume after disconnect?\n5. Which request paths must keep working while persistence or bridge dependencies are slow, locked, or stale?\n6. How can a CLI or test harness inspect the exact event sequence without the UI?\n7. Which headless scenario proves the happy path, failure path, recovery path, terminal state, and hot-path timeout/degraded path?\n8. Which client state consumes these events, and how does it prove ownership, freshness, completeness, ordering, and replay/resync?\n\nIf the answer is \"the UI can figure it out\", name the missing event instead.\n---\nname: learning-from-bugs\ndescription: Use when a meaningful bug, regression, architecture flaw, storage issue, memory problem, persistence failure, control-plane failure, or system-level failure has been diagnosed or fixed\n---\n\n# Learning From Bugs\n\nWhen a bug teaches something reusable, capture the lesson before moving on.\n\n## Use This For\n\nUse this after diagnosing or fixing bugs that involve:\n\n- architecture or ownership boundaries,\n- storage, persistence, migrations, caching, or file paths,\n- memory management, leaks, lifecycle, cleanup, or resource pressure,\n- concurrency, queues, retries, resumability, or recovery,\n- control planes, event streams, background workers, or long-running jobs,\n- security, data loss, user trust, or incident-like failures,\n- any bug that took repeated attempts or revealed a wrong mental model.\n\nSkip it for typos, obvious one-line UI mistakes, throwaway test fixture fixes, or purely local churn that will not help future work.\n\n## Required Output\n\nWrite a short learning note to:\n\n`docs/superpowers/learnings/YYYY-MM-DD-<bug-or-lesson-slug>.md`\n\nCreate the directory if needed.\n\nUse this shape:\n\n```markdown\n# [Lesson Title]\n\n**Date:** YYYY-MM-DD\n**Context:** [project, feature, or subsystem]\n**Symptom:** [what failed]\n**Root Cause:** [the real cause, not the symptom]\n**Fix:** [what changed]\n**Verification:** [commands, tests, or checks that proved it]\n**Prevention:** [what future agents should do differently]\n**Skill/Doc Updates:** [nearby skills or docs updated, or why no general update was needed]\n```\n\nKeep it concrete. Future agents should be able to read the note and avoid the same mistake.\n\n## Update The System When The Lesson Generalizes\n\nIf the bug reveals a reusable rule, update the nearest skill or defaults doc in the same change. Examples:\n\n- debugging lesson -> `systematic-debugging`\n- verification gap -> `verification-before-completion`\n- control-plane or eventing lesson -> `instrumenting-control-planes`\n- React lifecycle or routing lesson -> `building-react-apps`\n- planning omission -> `writing-plans` or `brainstorming`\n\nDo not bury a general lesson only in a project note. The learning note records the case; the skill update changes future behavior.\n\n## Completion Gate\n\nBefore saying a meaningful bug is fixed, check:\n\n1. Is this lesson reusable?\n2. Is there a learning note?\n3. Did any skill or defaults doc need an update?\n4. Did verification prove the fix?\n\nIf the answer to 1 is yes, do not skip the note. If the answer to 3 is no, say why in the note.\n"

## Codex progress · 2026-08-16T11:52:59.320Z

The app is back up now: both the UI/API on port 3050 and the agent bridge on 7800 return healthy responses.

The code also shows a second part of the failure: the 15-second watchdog can start another sweep before the previous one finishes, and any rejected sweep promise is left unhandled. I’m adding a focused test for both protections—one sweep at a time, and failure reporting without killing Node—before changing the implementation.

## Codex progress · 2026-08-16T11:54:22.613Z

The regression test now passes. The fix keeps watchdog sweeps single-file—if one is still running, the next tick shares it—and converts a failed sweep into a named diagnostic event plus a log entry instead of an unhandled rejection that terminates the server.

I’m doing the broader type/test checks now and recording the incident so the same process-lifecycle mistake is easy to recognize later.

<!-- /codex-event -->

const patch = "*** Begin Patch\n*** Add File: /Users/masterman/NLP/omniharness/docs/superpowers/learnings/2026-08-16-watchdog-sweeps-must-not-overlap-or-crash-runner.md\n+# Watchdog Sweeps Must Not Overlap or Crash the Runner\n+\n+**Date:** 2026-08-16\n+**Context:** OmniHarness supervisor runtime watchdog and SQLite-backed durable wake cleanup\n+**Symptom:** The production runner disappeared from port 3050 while the restart controller stayed alive. The last runner log entry was an uncaught `SQLITE_BUSY: database is locked` error from scheduled-wake cleanup.\n+**Root Cause:** The 15-second watchdog timer launched `syncRunningSupervision()` without tracking or catching its promise. Slow sweeps could overlap and increase database contention, and a rejection that remained after the SQLite retry budget became an unhandled promise rejection that terminated Node.\n+**Fix:** Scheduled watchdog calls now share one in-flight sweep, contain failures, emit `supervisor.watchdog_sweep_failed`, and write the failure to stderr. Startup synchronization still rejects normally so an invalid initial state cannot be hidden.\n+**Verification:** `pnpm exec vitest run tests/supervisor/runtime-watchdog-scheduling.test.ts tests/supervisor/runtime-watchdog.test.ts tests/server/db-retry.test.ts --reporter=dot`; runner and bridge health checks on ports 3050 and 7800.\n+**Prevention:** Every repeating async timer must define overlap behavior and handle its returned promise. Background maintenance failures must be observable without becoming process-wide unhandled rejections.\n+**Skill/Doc Updates:** No general skill update was needed because the existing control-plane guidance already requires bounded work, explicit failure events, and no silent background failures; this regression came from not applying those rules to the timer boundary.\n*** End Patch";
text(await tools.apply_patch(patch));

```

expect(second).toBe(first);\n\n    finishSweep();\n    await first;\n\n    await runSweep();\n    expect(sweep).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(2);\n  });\n\n  it(\"reports a failed background sweep without The last runner log entry was an uncaught `SQLITE_BUSY: database is locked` error from scheduled-wake cleanup.\n**Root Cause:** The 15-second watchdog timer launched `syncRunningSupervision()` without tracking or catching its promise. Slow sweeps could overlap and increase database contention, and a rejection that remained after the SQLite retry budget became an unhandled promise rejection that terminated Node.\n**Fix:** Scheduled watchdog calls now share one in-flight sweep, contain failures, emit `supervisor.watchdog_sweep_failed`, and write the failure to stderr. Startup synchronization still rejects normally so an invalid initial state cannot be hidden.\n**Verification:** `pnpm exec vitest run tests/supervisor/runtime-watchdog-scheduling.test.ts tests/supervisor/runtime-watchdog.test.ts tests/server/db-retry.test.ts tests/server/events/named-events.test.ts --reporter=dot` passed 27 tests; `pnpm typecheck` passed; five live health probes spanning more than one watchdog interval returned HTTP 200, with listeners present on ports 3050 and 7800.\n**Prevention:** Every repeating async timer must define overlap behavior and handle its returned promise. Background maintenance failures must be observable without becoming process-wide unhandled rejections.\n**Skill/Doc Updates:** No general skill update was needed because the existing control-plane guidance already requires bounded work, explicit failure events, and no silent background failures; this regression came from not applying those rules to the timer boundary.\n"

## Codex final · 2026-08-16T11:56:07.826Z

The server crashed at 13:47:57 because a watchdog cleanup hit `SQLITE_BUSY: database is locked`. Its rejected promise was unhandled, terminating Node; the restart controller remained alive but did not restart it.

I restarted the server and fixed the watchdog to prevent overlapping sweeps and safely report failures instead of crashing:

- UI/API: port 3050, HTTP 200
- Agent bridge: port 7800, healthy
- 27 regression tests passed
- Full TypeScript check passed

Changes: [runtime-watchdog.ts](/Users/masterman/NLP/omniharness/src/server/supervisor/runtime-watchdog.ts), [regression test](/Users/masterman/NLP/omniharness/tests/supervisor/runtime-watchdog-scheduling.test.ts), and [incident note](/Users/masterman/NLP/omniharness/docs/superpowers/learnings/2026-08-16-watchdog-sweeps-must-not-overlap-or-crash-runner.md).

## Codex progress · 2026-08-16T13:29:58.089Z

The evidence points to one underlying storage problem, not two unrelated UI glitches:

- Run `1532362831ad` exists and is still marked running, but its worker stream metadata write was blocked.
- Run `95314f1fc1d9` does not exist in `runs`, yet the server still tried to insert its first message, which explains the foreign-key failure.
- Both the main runner and the agent bridge currently have the same SQLite database open, and the database’s WAL file is unusually large (about 56 MB), so I’m tracing the long writer and the missing transaction boundary now.

The “Quore is working” sentence is composed dynamically rather than stored as that exact text, so I’m locating its translation key and status rule next.

<!-- codex-event:{"kind":"progress","timestamp":"2026-08-16T13:31:15.811Z","phase":"commentary"} -->
## Codex progress · 2026-08-16T13:31:15.811Z

I found the race that explains the foreign-key error: the client began polling the requested run ID while conversation creation was still between inserting the run and inserting its worker. The snapshot reconciler saw that half-created direct run as a “zombie”; seven seconds later, the create request tried to add the first message to a run that had already disappeared.

I’m confirming the exact deletion branch and then I’ll make creation atomic or protect the startup state so polling cannot destroy an in-progress run. The separate stream error was transient—the Dis3 worker kept writing and has advanced beyond the failed sequence—but it confirms the database is under enough write contention to widen this race.

## Codex progress · 2026-08-16T13:32:07.865Z

The exact cause is now clearer, and it is inside OmniHarness’s SQLite usage—not the Dis3 project.

At the same timestamp, OmniHarness logged several `cannot commit transaction - SQL statements in progress` failures. The run-creation path uses `INSERT … RETURNING` but reads it with `.get()`, which can leave the SQLite statement unfinished. Later writes then run on another connection: the worker entry reaches the JSONL stream, while the uncommitted run row is invisible, so the first message fails its foreign key and the partial transaction rolls back. I’m checking every occurrence of that unsafe pattern before changing the shared helper/path.

## Codex progress · 2026-08-16T13:32:34.540Z

I’m fixing it now. The immediate change is to stop using `.get()` on SQLite writes with `RETURNING`; those statements must be fully consumed before the connection can commit. I’m adding a regression that proves a second database connection can write immediately after worker-number allocation, then I’ll apply the same safe pattern to the other OmniHarness write-returning paths that can leave transactions open.

Split it. | `test('validates email and domain and whitespace')` |\n| **Clear** | Name describes behavior | `test('test1')` |\n| **Shows intent** | Demonstrates desired API | Obscures what code should do |\n\n## Why Order Matters\n\n**\"I'll write tests after to verify it works\"**\n\nTests written after code pass immediately. Passing immediately proves nothing:\n- Might test wrong thing\n- Might test implementation, not behavior\n- Might miss edge cases you forgot\n- You never saw it catch the bug\n\nTest-first forces you to see the test fail, proving it actually tests something.\n\n**\"I already manually tested all the edge cases\"**\n\nManual testing is ad-hoc. ## Codex progress · 2026-08-16T13:36:48.508Z

The first regression is fixed: worker-number allocation no longer leaves a write-with-`RETURNING` statement open, and account cleanup no longer puts seven `RETURNING` writes inside one SQLite batch. Those were the statements producing the exact commit error in the live event log.

I’m also making worker-stream metadata contention non-fatal. The JSONL entry is already safely on disk at that point, so a busy metadata cursor should be reported and retried by the next append—not shown as “Stream live agent state failed.”

I’m using the project’s debugging, database-state, and test-first guidance for this.

    "text": "     691 docs/architecture/lifecycle-observability-and-testing.md\n# Lifecycle Observability & Resilience Testing\n\n> What we keep getting wrong, why our tests don't catch it, and the discipline that fixes it.\n\nRelated: `docs/architecture/hot-path-responsiveness-and-resource-leaks.md`\ndocuments the May 2026 reload/worker-streaming latency incident and the\nresource-ownership rules for keeping page bootstrap, SSE, and worker stream\npaths responsive while agents are running.\n\n## Multi-runner client lifecycle\n\nEach saved runner profile owns one `RunnerConnection` state machine and at most\none main event stream. A registry starts every profile connection, not only the\nvisible one. Switching the visible workspace changes active managers/query\ncaches and terminal ownership without closing inactive main streams.\n\nEvery bootstrap, snapshot, frame, retry, timer, and mutation checks profile and\nlearned runner identity before applying state. Stored cursors include the\nrunner's stream epoch. `runner.stopping`, `auth.session_revoked`, and\n`stream.resync_required` are typed terminal/control outcomes, not generic\nnetwork failures.\n\nElectron, VS Code, and Capacitor host bridges have bounded stream delivery and\nmust cancel upstream work on overflow. Mobile suspension persists cursors,\ncloses streams, and reconnects on resume; it must not claim background\ndelivery. Platform lifecycle contract tests live under `tests/electron`,\n`tests/vscode`, `tests/mobile`, and `tests/runtime-api`; real two-runner and\neight-runner journeys live under `tests/e2e`.\n\n## Interactive protocol invariant\n\nAn advertised interactive agent capability is operational only when the complete user journey is implemented: receive the request, append it to the unified worker stream, render an actionable control in the main conversation, submit the exact protocol response, and append a terminal outcome before resolving the agent request. Side-panel-only controls do not satisfy this invariant. Every form shape and permission option emitted by a supported adapter must be covered by a finite wire-to-UI regression matrix.\n\nActionability comes only from the live runtime's `pendingElicitations` and\n`pendingPermissions`; an open worker-stream row proves only that a request\nexisted. After reattach or recreation, compare the durable open rows with the\nruntime-owned request ids and append terminal `cancelled` rows for any orphaned\nrequests before publishing the recovered worker. The UI may render the stream\nrows as history, but must never turn them back into response controls.\n\nRelated: `docs/architecture/timing-determinism-audit.md` records the May 20,\n2026 audit of race-prone frontend and control-plane patterns: cached snapshots\npretending to be authoritative, stale async callbacks, timer-owned actions,\ntimestamp-only ordering, and silent wake/lease contention.\n\n## Interrupted-turn recovery invariant\n\nReattaching a provider session restores conversation context; it does not prove\nthat the interrupted turn is running again. If a persisted active direct worker\nis missing after a runner restart and the reattached runtime comes back idle\nwithout a terminal stop reason or pending user input, recovery must explicitly\nsend a continuation prompt, keep the run `running`, and persist the eventual\nturn result. The continuation runs as an owned background conversation task so\nsnapshot bootstrap does not block on the agent turn. A newer user turn may\nsupersede it, but that decision must resolve the recovery incident and emit a\nnamed event.\n\nAn intentional stop or steer abort is a successful ownership handoff, not a\nworker failure. Older initial-turn handlers must recognize the abort and must\nnot emit `run_failed` or overwrite the replacement turn's status. Every queue\nrow claimed by the interrupted delivery must leave `delivering`: close it as\ndelivered if its exact message id reached the transcript, otherwise return it\nto pending. An elicitation answer resumes the turn that already owns the live\nquestion, so it must never wait behind that same turn's per-worker gate; doing\nso is a self-deadlock because the turn cannot finish until the answer arrives.\n\n## Why this document exists\n\nOver a single afternoon we hit three production-class bugs that the existing test\nsuite did not catch and could not have caught:\n\n1. **Session fails to reconnect after a server restart and gives up after the\n   first attempt.** No user-visible message, no telemetry event, no recovery\n   incident — just a silently dead session.\n2. **`DELETE /conversations/:id` fails with a foreign-key constraint** because\n   related rows in dependent tables were not cleared first. The error surfaces\n   as an opaque 500.\n3. **Running plan-improvement agents fails because leftover state blocks the\n   new run.** The block is silent; the user sees nothing happen and assumes the\n   button is broken.\n\nThese are not unrelated bugs. They share a single root cause:\n\n> **The server makes state transitions that nobody observes.** Neither the user,\n> nor the UI, nor any test client can tell what the server decided. So bugs in\n> the *decision* (gave up too early, took the wrong branch, refused silently)\n> are invisible.\n\nThis document records what we learned and the rules we now follow so that this\nclass of bug stops shipping.\n\nRelated incident note: `docs/architecture/supervisor-worker-switching-incident.md`\nrecords the worker-switching failure from session `690d2fa9f2a7`, where\n`awaiting_user` was treated as runnable, Gemini workers were live but persisted\nas `starting`, and duplicate continuation workers were spawned.\n\nRelated direct-control note:\n`docs/architecture/direct-control-session-regressions.md` records the\n`ffb912d4d5d7`, `937e642f3535`, and `734cc38f4d7f` regressions around\nlifecycle noise, stale queued send-now state, missing unified-stream worker\noutput, and permanent \"Thinking...\" indicators.\n\nRelated state-staleness note:\n`docs/architecture/state-staleness-and-session-lifecycle-lessons.md` records\nthe `0785684884fa`, `14260d2a2df0`, `ecea142f7344`, and `18fc406457f3`\nregressions around stale SSE/cache payloads, queued-message races, direct-run\nstatus classification, unread markers, and worker-stream loading.\n\n---\n\n## What we found in the audit\n\nA targeted audit of `src/app/api/events/route.ts` plus the planning, recovery,\nand bridge-client subsystems revealed the structural gaps.\n\n### 1. The SSE stream is a snapshot stream, not an event stream\n\n`/api/events` emits exactly one named event: `update`, whose payload is the\n*entire* current state of the world for the selected run (messages, plans,\nruns, workers, planItems, clarifications, executionEvents, supervisor\ninterventions, queued messages, recovery incidents, review runs/rounds/findings).\n\nThere are no other named events. An observer cannot ask \"did a worker spawn?\"\nor \"was a recovery attempted?\" — only \"is the state now different?\" To answer\nthe first kind of question the client must **diff snapshots**, which is:\n\n- **Ambiguous** — many transitions produce identical visible state (a worker\n  that was reattached and a worker that was recreated both end up as\n  `status=\"running\"`).\n- **Lossy** — fast transitions can be coalesced inside a single snapshot\n  interval and disappear entirely. (e.g. `starting → running → completed`\n  inside one 15s window.)\n- **Forced to re-derive server decisions** — the client has to reconstruct\n  *why* state changed, which requires duplicating server logic.\n\n### 2. There is no event ID and no resume\n\nThe SSE frames have no `id:` field. There is no `Last-Event-ID` handling on the\nserver. A client that disconnects and reconnects gets a fresh snapshot and has\n*no way to know* whether events fired during the gap. For chaos testing (where\nwe deliberately drop the connection) this is fatal — we cannot assert\n\"between t0 and t1 the server emitted [X, Y, Z]\" because the wire format does\nnot carry that information.\n\nThere is a `?snapshot=1` bootstrap endpoint, which is good. There is no\n\"give me the events I missed since id N\" endpoint, which is the gap.\n\n### 3. Several decisions are invisible to the wire\n\nConcrete state transitions that **the server makes** but **never tells anyone\nabout**:\n\n| Transition | Where it happens | Wire visibility |\n|---|---|---|\n| Worker spawned | `bridge-client/index.ts spawnAgent` | None — inferred from a row appearing |\n| Worker reattached vs recreated after restart | `restart-control.ts` / recovery path | **None** — both look like `status=\"running\"` |\n| Recovery gave up after N attempts | `recoveryIncidents.autoAttemptCount` increments | Partial — count is visible but there is no terminal \"abandoned\" state |\n| Plan readiness reached | `derivePlanningStatus()` — runs **client-side** | **None** — it is a client-side derivation, not a server event |\n| Plan-improvement blocked by leftover state | `planning/review.ts` early-return | **None** — silent refusal |\n| Conversation delete FK violation | `/api/conversations/[id]` DELETE | None as a typed event — only a 500 response |\n| Message ack / persisted / streaming chunk | `conversations/send-message.ts` | Partial — only the resulting queued-message status |\n\nEvery row in this table is a bug class waiting to ship. If the server can\nsilently decide \"I gave up\", \"I refused\", \"I took branch B not A\", and the\ntest harness has no way to assert which branch it took, the test harness is\nstructurally incapable of catching the bug.\n\n### 4. The user-facing surface mirrors the test-facing surface\n\nThe reason \"leftover state blocked the run\" did not show a user message is the\n**same reason** no test could detect it: there was no event for it. Make the\nstate transitions observable, and both the UI fix and the test coverage\nfollow. Conversely, if a transition is observable only by re-deriving from a\nsnapshot diff, both the UI and tests will be brittle in the same ways.\n\nThis is the central insight: **observability for users and observability for\ntests are the same problem**.\n\n### 5. Playwright e2e is the wrong layer for resilience\n\nThe existing `tests/e2e/*.spec.ts` files boot Chromium. They are slow (tens of\nseconds per scenario), flaky against real subprocess restarts, and they\nexercise UI rendering rather than control-plane decisions. The bugs we are\nhitting are not UI bugs — they are control-plane bugs. We should be hitting\nHTTP/SSE directly, in Node, with no browser. The UI is one consumer of the\ncontrol plane; the chaos harness is another.\n\n---\n\n## The rules we now follow\n\nThese are not suggestions. They are the discipline that makes this class of\nbug stop happening.\n\n### Rule 1: every server-side state transition emits a named event\n\nIf the server makes a decision — spawn, reattach, recreate, give up, refuse,\ndelete, fail — that decision is published on the event stream with a\n**named event type**, not just a state delta. Examples:\n\n- `worker.spawned`, `worker.status` (with `prev` and `next`), `worker.terminal`\n- `worker.reattached`, `worker.recreated`\n- `plan.ready`, `plan.review.started`, `plan.review.finished`,\n  `plan.review.blocked` (with a `reason`)\n- `recovery.opened`, `recovery.attempt`, `recovery.gave_up`, `recovery.resolved`\n- `conversation.deleted`, `conversation.delete_failed` (with FK details)\n- `error.surfaced` — the catch-all for anything the user should know about\n\n**Rule of thumb:** if a server method has an early-return, a try/catch that\nswallows, or a branch that depends on a state check, it emits an event.\n\"Silent\" is a code smell.\n\n### Rule 2: errors that affect the user are events, not just response codes\n\nA 500 with a body is not enough. A 200 that quietly did nothing is worse. Every\nuser-relevant failure publishes `error.surfaced` with a stable code, a\nhuman-readable message, and the relevant run/worker/conversation ids. The UI's\njob is to render `error.surfaced` events into toasts/banners. The test\nharness's job is to assert that the expected `error.surfaced` event fired.\n\nA failure that does not produce an `error.surfaced` event is a bug — even if\nthe underlying behaviour is technically correct — because it is invisible to\nthe user and to the tests.\n\nThe event carries the stable id of the subject that failed. Conversation and\nworker failures use `runId`, `conversationId`, or `workerId`; account-only\nsettings failures use `accountId` rather than pretending an account is a\nconversation.\n\n### Rule 3: the event stream is SSE-spec compliant\n\n- Every frame has an `id:` field. IDs are monotonic.\n- The server keeps a bounded **ring buffer** (≥ 500 entries) of recent events.\n- The server honours `Last-Event-ID` on reconnect: it replays everything after\n  that id from the buffer, then resumes live streaming.\n- If the requested id has fallen out of the buffer, the server emits a\n  `stream.resync_required` event so the client knows to re-bootstrap from\n  `?snapshot=1` rather than silently miss events.\n\nThis is the SSE spec. We were not following it. We are now.\n\n### Rule 4: named events alongside, not instead of, snapshots\n\nThe existing `update` snapshot event stays. The UI keeps consuming it. The new\nnamed events are *additional* frames on the same stream. Clients that don't\ncare about a given event type ignore it. There is no `?test=1` flag, no\nseparate test endpoint, no parallel surface that can drift.\n\nA new named event is not client-visible merely because the server emits it.\nIts regression test must prove the complete delivery chain: the EventSource\nadapter subscribes to the exact event name, the runtime stream normalizer\npreserves that name as `kind`, and the owning client manager dispatches the\nbounded payload. Test at least one real named frame through this chain; handler\nunit tests alone cannot detect an omitted subscription or a normalizer that\ndrops the event kind.\n\nA committed control-plane row proves durable intent, not delivery to an\nexternal worker or event consumer. Any post-commit side effect must have one\nordering owner, a durable delivery marker, a retry wake-up mechanism, startup\nrecovery, and a last-moment canonical fence. Idempotent request replay must\n"

The UI may or may not consume the event. That is a separate choice. const patch = "*** Begin Patch\n*** Add File: /Users/masterman/NLP/omniharness/docs/superpowers/learnings/2026-08-16-sqlite-returning-batches-block-commits.md\n+# SQLite `RETURNING` statements can block later commits\n+\n+## Date\n+\n+2026-08-16\n+\n+## Context\n+\n+OmniHarness creates a run, allocates its first worker number, refreshes the account inventory, appends the first worker-stream entry, and then inserts the user's initial message. These operations share the local libSQL/SQLite client with worker-stream metadata updates.\n+\n+## Symptom\n+\n+A live worker-stream cursor update failed with `SQLITE_BUSY: database is locked`. Seconds later, creating another conversation failed while inserting its initial message with `SQLITE_CONSTRAINT: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed`. At the same timestamp, account cleanup emitted repeated `cannot commit transaction - SQL statements in progress` errors.\n+\n+## Root cause\n+\n+Two write paths used data-changing statements with `RETURNING`:\n+\n+- worker-number allocation used an upsert with `RETURNING ... .get()`;\n+- deleted-account cleanup submitted seven `UPDATE`/`DELETE ... RETURNING` statements through `db.batch()`.\n+\n+With the local libSQL driver, those result-producing write statements could remain active while the transaction tried to commit. That blocked the commit, increased write contention, and allowed conversation creation to reach later persistence steps without a reliably committed parent run.\n+\n+Separately, worker-stream JSONL bytes were already flushed before the SQLite metadata cursor update. Treating a busy cursor update as an append failure incorrectly surfaced a live-stream error even though the transcript entry was safe on disk.\n+\n+## Fix\n+\n+- Worker-number allocation now performs a non-returning upsert and reads the allocated number inside the same retried transaction.\n+- Deleted-account cleanup uses non-returning batch statements and checks `rowsAffected`.\n+- A busy artifact cursor update is now deferred after the durable append, emits `artifact.metadata_update_deferred`, and advances the in-process sequence cursor so the next append cannot reuse a sequence number. Non-busy metadata failures still propagate.\n+\n+## Verification\n+\n+- Regression tests assert that worker allocation and account-cleanup batches contain no `RETURNING` clause.\n+- A stream-metadata regression test forces `SQLITE_BUSY`, verifies that the durable append is accepted, verifies the diagnostic event, and verifies that the next reserved sequence advances.\n+- The relevant account, worker-id, artifact, output-store, event, conversation-route, and type-check suites are run before deployment.\n+\n+## Prevention\n+\n+- Do not use DML `RETURNING` in local SQLite transaction or batch paths when a follow-up `SELECT` inside the same transaction can provide the value.\n+- A durable append and its derived metadata cursor have different failure semantics. The durable bytes are authoritative; a recoverable metadata lock should be observable and retried/caught up, not reported as lost content.\n+- Tests for append recovery must assert both durability and sequence monotonicity.\n+\n+## Skill/Doc Updates\n+\n+This incident reinforces the append-only artifact-stream rules in `docs/architecture/lifecycle-observability-and-testing.md`: JSONL is the durable content authority, SQLite stores its cursor, and metadata failures need typed named events.\n*** End Patch";
text(await tools.apply_patch(patch));

## Codex final · 2026-08-16T13:44:37.021Z

Fixed and deployed in the running OmniHarness server.

Cause: SQLite couldn’t finish account-cleanup and worker-allocation transactions because they used `RETURNING` statements. The parent run was rolled back, so inserting its first message triggered the foreign-key failure.

Changes:

- Removed problematic `RETURNING` operations in [migration.ts](/Users/masterman/NLP/omniharness/src/server/accounts/migration.ts).
- Made worker-number allocation atomic and retryable in [ids.ts](/Users/masterman/NLP/omniharness/src/server/workers/ids.ts).
- Made transient stream-metadata locks recoverable in [stream-metadata.ts](/Users/masterman/NLP/omniharness/src/server/artifacts/stream-metadata.ts).
- Added unit and lifecycle regressions plus an [incident note](/Users/masterman/NLP/omniharness/docs/superpowers/learnings/2026-08-16-sqlite-returning-batches-block-commits.md).

Verification:

- 103 focused server tests passed.
- 49 lifecycle tests passed.
- Typecheck passed.
- SQLite integrity check passed.
- UI and agent bridge both return HTTP 200.
- No database-lock or foreign-key errors since restart.

Dis3 was not lost: it reached sequence 8,718 and is now marked done. You can retry creating the failed conversation.
